Dyothelitism
dai-oh-THEL-i-tiz-um
noun (Christology)
From Greek dyo (two) + thelema (will); the orthodox doctrine, defined at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681), that Christ has two wills — a divine will and a human will — corresponding to His two natures. Opposed to monothelitism (the heresy that Christ has only one will).

📖 Biblical Definition

From Greek dyo (two) + thelema (will); the orthodox Christological doctrine that Christ has two wills — a divine will and a human will — corresponding to His two natures, the human will being in perfect, unconfused submission to and harmony with the divine will. The doctrine was defined at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681, the Sixth Ecumenical Council) against the heresy of monothelitism (from monos, one, + thelema, will), which held that Christ has only one will. The logic of dyothelitism follows from the two-natures doctrine of Chalcedon: a complete human nature includes a human will (the will being a faculty of the nature, not merely of the person); therefore the complete human nature of Christ includes a complete human will, distinct from His divine will; Christ has two wills, corresponding to His two natures. The biblical foundation is principally the agony in Gethsemane, where Christ's human will and the divine will are distinctly expressed yet in perfect harmony: O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt (Matthew 26:39; cf. Luke 22:42, not my will, but thine, be done). The distinction between my will (the human will of Christ, naturally recoiling from the cup of suffering and wrath) and thy will (the divine will, to which the human will perfectly submits) displays the two wills in their distinct operation and perfect harmony. Dyothelitism guards the integrity and completeness of Christ's human nature (a human nature without a human will would be incomplete, and the redemption of the human will would be unaccomplished, on the principle that what is not assumed is not healed). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive orthodox doctrine of dyothelitism: Christ has two wills, divine and human, corresponding to His two natures, the human will in perfect submission to and harmony with the divine; this preserves the completeness of His humanity (including the redemption of the human will, displayed in Gethsemane's not my will, but thine, be done) and the integrity of the two-natures Christology.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

From Greek dyo (two) + thelema (will); the orthodox doctrine (Third Council of Constantinople, 680-681) that Christ has two wills — divine and human — corresponding to His two natures, the human will in perfect submission to the divine; displayed in Gethsemane (not my will, but thine, be done); opposed to monothelitism.

DYOTHELITISM, n. (Christology; Greek dyo [two] + thelema [will]) Christ has two wills — a divine will and a human will — corresponding to His two natures, the human will in perfect, unconfused submission to and harmony with the divine. Defined at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681, Sixth Ecumenical Council) against monothelitism (one will). The logic follows from Chalcedon: a complete human nature includes a human will (a faculty of the nature); Christ's complete human nature includes a human will distinct from His divine will. Biblical foundation: Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39, not as I will, but as thou wilt; Luke 22:42, not my will, but thine, be done). Guards the completeness of Christ's humanity (what is not assumed is not healed).

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 26:39 — "And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."

Luke 22:42 — "Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done."

John 6:38 — "For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me."

Hebrews 10:7 — "Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Dyothelitism (two wills in Christ) is the orthodox doctrine; opposed to monothelitism (one will), which compromises the completeness of Christ's human nature; the human will of Christ is in perfect submission to the divine will, displayed in Gethsemane.

expand to see more

Dyothelitism is held against the heresy of monothelitism (one will in Christ). Monothelitism arose in the seventh century as an attempt at compromise with the monophysites (who held one nature in Christ); it conceded two natures but held that Christ has only one will (a single divine-human will, or a will belonging only to the divine Person). The orthodox church rejected monothelitism at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681) on the substantive ground that it compromises the completeness of Christ's human nature: the will is a faculty of the nature (not merely of the person), so that a complete human nature must include a complete human will; a Christ with only one will would lack a complete human nature, and the redemption of the human will (which fell in Adam and must be redeemed in Christ) would be unaccomplished — on the patristic principle that what is not assumed is not healed (Gregory of Nazianzus), the human will must be assumed by Christ to be redeemed. The biblical foundation for dyothelitism is principally the agony in Gethsemane, where Christ's human will and the divine will are distinctly expressed yet in perfect harmony: not my will, but thine, be done (Luke 22:42). The distinction between Christ's human will (naturally recoiling from the cup of suffering) and the divine will (to which the human will perfectly submits) displays the two wills. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive orthodox doctrine: Christ has two wills, divine and human, corresponding to His two natures, the human will in perfect submission to and harmony with the divine; this preserves the completeness of His humanity and the integrity of the two-natures Christology, and displays the perfect obedience of the incarnate Son, whose human will, though it naturally shrank from the cross, perfectly submitted to the Father's will for our redemption.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dyo + thelema; two wills in Christ (divine and human); Third Council of Constantinople (680-681); against monothelitism; displayed in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42); guards the completeness of Christ's humanity.
